Thermal Pleasure and Alliesthesia in the Built Environment
Thomas Parkinson
A thesis submitted in fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy
Faculty of Architecture, Design and Planning

Abstract
Comfort surveys of building occupants the world over consistently report overall building
thermal satisfaction ratings hovering around the same 80% threshold set as the target nearly
50 years ago. But the general consensus emerging from the last two decades of thermal
comfort research is that constancy may not be the optimum mode of control for building
occupants and that thermal neutrality may even be detrimental to thermal satisfaction. The
steady-state models that have held sway over indoor climate practices in the second half of
the 20th century were never intended for use in dynamic or spatially non-isothermal indoor
thermal environments. New insight is required into understanding the perceptual processes
leading to a particular thermal environment being experienced as comfortable for some, but
distinctly uncomfortable for others.
The aim of this thesis is to propose the physiological concept of alliesthesia as a suitable
framework for understanding thermal environmental perception under dynamic or non-
isothermal conditions. Paper 1 outlines the theoretical basis of the alliesthesia hypothesis. The
presumption that discomfort is required before any pleasure can be derived from thermal
stimuli is challenged through a systematic review of contemporary physiological theory that
has superseded the control theory upon which the original alliesthesia concept was based.
This is followed by the presentation and discussion of empirical evidence from a series of
human-subject laboratory experiments (Papers 2 - 4) that lend support to the alliesthesia
hypothesis for perception of nonsteady-state, innocuous thermal environments.
The principal conclusion is that strong subjective discomfort is not a necessary precondition
for thermal pleasure. Alliesthesia remained viable even within the physiological
thermoneutral zone, although it was less pronounced and more ambiguous in those moderate
scenarios. Yet there is significant potential in moderate, everyday indoor environments to
leverage the alliesthesia concept through peripheral thermal stimulation. Positive hedonic
tones were elicited during innocuous exposures at the margins of the thermal comfort zone by
applying moderate local skin temperature changes that were contrapuntal to the whole-body,
mean skin temperature. This phenomenon was termed ‘spatial alliesthesia.’ Observations of
local skin temperature during asymmetric exposures indicate that the underlying mechanism
driving a spatial alliesthesial response is the dynamic discharge rate of cutaneous
thermoreceptors.
Paper 3 and 4 investigated reverse instances of local discomfort (thermal pleasure) on the
fringes of the comfort zone and interpreted the results through the spatial alliesthesia
i

framework. In both warm and cool conditions, whole-body thermal pleasure was elicited from
locally applied stimuli that contrast the whole-body thermal state. However, the hedonic tone
attached to thermal environmental stimuli, both localised and whole-body, exhibited
pronounced between-subject variability. A MANOVA tested between-group differences of
psychological and physiological parameters deemed to be relevant to the spatial alliesthesia
hypothesis. The most useful variable for distinguishing the tone and magnitude of thermal
pleasure response to localised thermal stimuli was the intensity of the subjects’ displeasure in
the preconditioning environment. The magnitude of change in local skin temperature also had
a significant effect on perceived pleasantness of localised thermal stimuli. This result
indicates that the hedonic valence attached to stimuli will be different between occupants
depending on their physiological state and thermal preference.
A binomial logistic regression model was developed to ascertain whether measured
parameters could inform a predictive model of spatial alliesthesia. Initial skin temperature and
initial thermal pleasure status were shown to very good predictors of the hedonic response to
localised warming, in some instances improving correct prediction close to 90%. This result
suggests it may therefore be possible to develop a model of spatial alliesthesial response to
stimuli following more extensive experimentation with the potential for positive alliesthesia
to deliver thermal delight within built environments.
Whilst the concept of thermal alliesthesia is yet to be fully articulated, the findings emanating
from this thesis could start the discussion on how it could be leveraged in the provision of
thermal comfort in nonsteady-state environments. It may be possible to increase occupant
satisfaction whilst simultaneously reducing energy consumption through the correct
implementation of targeted thermal stimulation delivered locally by personal environmental
control (PEC) systems. PEC systems offer an excellent solution to understand how spatial
alliesthesia may be elicited in free-living environments, and future research on the topic
should aim to explore this avenue of application.

Introduction
It has been estimated that inhabitants of countries in the developed world spend more than
90% of their daily lives inside built environments (e.g. Klepeis et al., 2001), most often in
mechanically conditioned spaces where indoor climates have been stripped of temporal or
spatial variability. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems
maintaining that thermal constancy are widely recognised as the single largest energy end-use
within the commercial buildings sector (e.g. Perez-Lombard et al., 2008). The energy demand
of HVAC is amplified by the narrow temperature deadbands programmed into building
management systems, irrespective of prevailing weather, climatic context, or cultural
characteristics (Hoyt et al., 2015). The climatically disruptive greenhouse gas emissions that
can be directly attributed to the maintenance of isothermal and unvarying indoor climates are
undeniable (ürge-Vorsatz et al., 2007).
Excessive HVAC energy demand in the built environment appears to be less a technological
challenge than a behavioural and psychological one (IPCC, 2007). Continual enhancements in
the energy efficiency of HVAC systems are steadily eroded by escalating thermal
expectations of building occupants. Notwithstanding the technical capability of modern
HVAC systems to deliver on the promise of thermal constancy, comfort surveys of building
occupants the world over (de Dear, 1998) consistently report overall building thermal
satisfaction ratings hovering around the same 80% threshold set as the target nearly 50 years
ago by the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-conditioning Engineers
(Arens et al., 2010). This somewhat dismal observation prompts critical questions about the
net benefit of the prodigious energy inputs and technological enhancements to building
services.
The design goal of HVAC engineers is overtly to render the thermal realm inside buildings
imperceptible (Pallasmaa, 2013). Indeed the International Standards Organisation standard on
thermal comfort provides a performance assessment procedure that rates buildings using
thermal imperceptibility as the main performance criterion (ISO, 2005). Yet the human
thermosensory system provides sharp perceptual acuity of environmental stimuli, and an
autonomic thermoregulatory system to match, and combined together they are able to
equilibrate any perturbation to the body’s heat balance with its thermal environment. It is not
surprising that ‘exercising’ the body’s physiological thermoregulation system through
environmental stimulation and metabolic challenge is an important aspect of a healthy
lifestyle (van Marken Lichtenbelt & Kingma, 2013). Furthermore there is a hedonic
dimension to thermal stimulation as well, although it is often ignored (Cabanac, 1971).
1
1

Basking in the warm glow of sunlight on a brisk morning, or the languid caress of sea breeze
on a balmy summers afternoon are familiar examples of quotidian thermal delight.
Deliberately engineering any form of thermal stimulation out of an indoor climate is a
somewhat surprising goal for the design professions to be pursuing with such determination
and energy. And yet the international comfort design and compliance standards such as the
American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-conditioning Engineers’ Standard-55
(ASHRAE, 2013) and ISO-7730 (ISO, 2005) explicitly aim to minimise or eradicate the
thermal textures of buildings. Indeed, buildings can have their ratings downgraded in the
comfort standards if they fail to maintain isothermal constancy. But thermal asymmetries and
vertical gradients are common in air conditioned buildings (e.g. solar ingress through glazed
facades or localised internal sources of heating or cooling), and occupants also experience
diverse thermal exposure sequences as they move about their buildings’ internal
environments. A large share of extant thermal comfort literature has carried a punitive
disposition towards non-steady-state conditions (e.g. Fanger, 1970; Melikov & Nielsen, 1989;
Olesen et al., 1972), and this is reflected in the way comfort standards address thermal
inhomogeneities such as radiant asymmetry, vertical gradients, draft, floor surface
temperature, temperature cycles, ramps and drifts. This legacy underpins the one-size-fits-all,
neutral-as-optimum thermal comfort design goal.
But the general consensus emerging from the last two decades of thermal comfort research is
that constancy may not be the optimum mode of control for building occupants (e.g. de Dear
et al., 2013), and that thermal neutrality may even be detrimental to thermal satisfaction.
Field-studies of comfort inside buildings repeatedly demonstrate how that approach to the
provision of thermal comfort is fundamentally flawed (e.g. Arens et al., 2010; de Dear &
Brager, 1998), and against the backdrop of global climate change, relentless pursuit of
constant and isothermal indoor climates through energy-intensive mechanical systems is
extremely irresponsible. It seems timely then, to think beyond the unrealistic goal of
eradicating all trace of thermal sensation inside buildings, and instead direct attention towards
the potential for the complex thermal textures created by the built environment to excite the
senses and elicit thermal delight and pleasure (Heschong, 1979).
The task requires new insight into the perceptual processes leading to a particular thermal
environment being experienced as comfortable for some, but distinctly uncomfortable for
others. Littered throughout thermal comfort discourse are eloquent arguments and ineluctable
research evidence against the conventional “one-size-fits-all” approach to indoor climate
2
2

engineering (e.g. Brager et al., 2015). And we can see the recent research interest in personal
environmental control systems (e.g. Melikov, 2004; Zhang et al, 2015) as a deliberate design
shift away from the universal, constant and isothermal indoor environment towards something
more bespoke and nuanced. But what’s missing from these trends is an overarching
conceptual framework that connects these disparate research findings and provides a coherent
interpretation (de Dear, 2011). The steady-state models that have held sway over indoor
climate practices in the second half of the 20th century were never intended for use in dynamic
or spatially non-isothermal indoor thermal environments.
The principal objective of this thesis is to propose the physiological concept of alliesthesia,
originally defined by Cabanc (1971), as a suitable framework for understanding thermal
environmental perception under dynamic or non-isothermal conditions. I argue that
alliesthesia provides a sound conceptual basis to explain thermal comfort beyond
conventional steady-state notions to something more closely aligned with the
neurophysiological mechanisms actually responsible for human thermal sensation. There is a
clear focus in this thesis on the affective, hedonic dimensions of our experience of dynamic
and non-isothermal environments, and this reflects the important phenomenological
distinction between thermally neutral sensations and pleasure. While it has been largely
unexplored in the context of the built environment, thermal pleasure sits at the core of this
project. The overwhelming majority of extant thermal comfort research to date has focused on
the descriptive (thermal sensation) dimension of thermal perception, but very little attention
has been given to the affective layer of our thermal experiences. The use of psychometric
scales for hedonic valence is largely unexplored in the built environment research literature,
and has generally been confined to small scale physiological investigations of alliesthesia
(e.g. Attia & Engel, 1982; Cabanac, 1971, Mower, 1976; Winslow et al., 1937).
In line with Cabanac’s (1992) hypothesis that positioned pleasure as the ‘currency’ of
alliesthesia, thermal pleasure is used in this thesis to explore the hedonic tones attached to
thermal transients and spatially non-isothermal stimuli. But apart from just maintaining
consistency with the psychophysiological foundations of alliesthesia, thermal pleasure
appears intuitively to be a better psychometric scale than thermal comfort. Thermal sensation
is the default psychometric used in objective evaluations of thermal stimuli, and it is often
accompanied by the subjective assessment of thermal comfort on a 5-, 7-, or 9-point Likert
scale. As per the ASHRAE definition, thermal comfort is a “condition of mind”, indicating it
is an evaluative process and therefore includes consideration of factors beyond the physical
environment, such as happiness and health. Pleasure, or pleasantness, is different in that it
3
3

directly addresses the affective component of the environmental stimulus. Within the realm of
hedonic psychology, affect is considered basic because it is an irreducible component of all
phenomena within the global affective domain (Ekkekakis, 2003). Comfort is a higher-order
evaluation that considers many factors, whilst pleasure is considered to be low-level or
‘primal’ because of its role in interpreting the ‘usefulness’ of a stimulus for regulation of all
of our homeostatic systems. Using evaluations of sensation and pleasure instead of comfort
holds teleological appeal because the interpretation of perceptual processes through an
alliesthesial framework is better understood through the mechanisms of the thermosensory
system rather than a condition of mind.
The structure of this thesis departs from the conventional format, in that the research was
conceived and performed as a multi-part series on alliesthesia. Therefore, the body of the
thesis is comprised solely of papers accepted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal. Each
paper is a stand-alone work covering a particular phase in the research project, but
connections to other entries in the series are made through the overarching narrative of the
thesis. The material is sequenced to gradually enlarge the field-of-view of core concept of the
thesis, thermal alliesthesia:
• Paper one: the theoretical underpinnings of thermosensation in the context of the built
environment;
• Paper two: presentation of empirical data describing whole-body alliesthesia during
sequential temperature step-changes;
• Paper three: experiments testing for spatial alliesthesia in asymmetrical exposures on
the lower fringe of the comfort zone.
• Paper four: experiments testing for spatial alliesthesia in asymmetrical exposures on
the upper fringe of the comfort zone.
Figure 1 schematically presents the conceptual foundation of the project and places each
paper within the context of the physiological and perceptual zones that were theoretically
defined and empirically tested.
4
4

Figure 1. A conceptual representation of the proposed coupling between thermal perception
and thermophysiology. The ‘alliesthesial type’ is superimposed within each zone, as per the
findings of the papers listed within the figure.
The first paper (physiology of alliesthesia) introduces the physiological concept of
alliesthesia through an extensive literature review of foundational and contemporary
thermophysiological theories, neuroscientific investigations of thermosensation, thermal
comfort research including the related engineering design and compliance standards. The aim
of this paper is to form the theoretical basis of my central hypothesis: that alliesthesia
provides a unifying framework to understand thermal perception in the built environment that
reconciles the disparate and often contradictory strands of thermal comfort research under
non-steady-state and non-isothermal conditions. It also proposes a refinement of the thermal
alliesthesia concept into whole-body (temporal) and spatial variants of thermal pleasure. This
conceptual dichotomy frames the experimental work of the three subsequent papers.
The second paper (alliesthesia in different regulatory zones) details the first human-
subject experiments in which alliesthesia is explored across the various thermophysiological
zones depicted in Figure 1 above. The aim of the experiment is to demonstrate that positive
alliesthesia occurs within the physiological thermoneutral zone. Thermal pleasure responses
from 13 university-aged subjects (six women, seven men) in nonsteady-state conditions are
characterised during a series of temperature transitions, drifts, and asymmetries designed to
simulate everyday thermal exposures. Attention is given to the role of both skin (T , dT ,

The third paper (spatial alliesthesia from contact heating) zeroes in on spatial alliesthesia
by examining reverse instances of the widely research local discomfort phenomenon. 53
university-aged subjects (20 women, 33 men) undergo contact heating of the hands and feet
(5 and 10-minutes respectively) on exposed skin. Local heating is used to test for spatial
alliesthesia experienced by subjects when exposed to ambient temperatures on the lower
margin of the comfort zone (T = 21.5°C). The principal aim is to determine if whole-body

The fourth paper (spatial alliesthesia from air movement) continues the investigation of
spatial alliesthesia by testing positive affective responses from 35 university-aged subjects
(nine women, 26 men) to increased air movement (0.4-0.9 m/s) in ambient temperatures
towards the upper fringe of the comfort zone (T = 27.5°C). Positive pleasure under

findings for the design and specification of personal environmental control systems in warm

The concluding section of the thesis summarises the findings of the individual research
papers in the broader context of the alliesthesia hypothesis and its role in thermal perception
in innocuous indoor climatic exposures.
